title: US strikes Iranian oil tankers as Tehran targets American base in Jordan
description: US forces struck five Iranian tankers on Tuesday, sinking one, in response to Tehran twice targeting an American warship, US Central Command (Centcom)
body: US forces struck five Iranian tankers on Tuesday, sinking one, in response to Tehran twice targeting an American warship, US Central Command (Centcom) said.Four Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) were targeted, as well as another near Kharg Island, a major oil terminal off Iran's coast, Centcom added.Tehran responded by launching missiles at a US base in Jordan - most of which were shot down - and said it attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.Tit-for-tat strikes between the two countries have escalated in the past week, more than six months after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February.Oil prices rose in Asia trading. Benchmark Brent crude was up by 1.5% at $99.35 (£73.35) a barrel, while US-traded oil was 1.3% higher at $94.23.Jordan said it had shot down 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, while two of them fell in unpopulated areas, an official spokesperson for the Jordanian Armed Forces said. After warning of further retaliatory strikes, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they had attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers and 10 "non-compliant vessels" trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported.The latest round of escalation comes after Iran targeted a US warship with ballistic missiles, which Centcom said were "successfully evaded". It added that no American troops were harmed during the attacks.In response, the US said that the five Iranian oil tankers it targeted were "part of a multi-billion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies".One of the ships it had struck, the M/T Riesco, sunk in the Gulf of Oman, Centcom later said, posting a video on X of the damaged vessel. Kharg Island - where one Iranian tanker was attacked in the latest round of US strikes - hosts Iran's main terminal for exporting oil. Some 90% of the country's crude oil passes through the island in the Gulf, transported through pipes from the mainland.Pressure on oil prices has been exacerbated by wider regional instability. Also on Tuesday, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement attacked energy facilities and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 people, according to Saudi authorities.The drone and missile attack caused fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry said.When asked by reporters about the latest tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the situation was "pretty straightforward"."Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And, for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters during a trip in Colombia.The US strikes on Tuesday came hours after Iran's navy claimed it had seized an uncrewed US submarine in the Strait of Hormuz.US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, said that the "underwater drone operated by US forces malfunctioned more than a day ago" and was used to survey regional waters "in support of ongoing operations".The defective drone was "an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment", he said, adding that US operations in regional waters were ongoing.With additional reporting from Peter Hoskins.

schema.headline: US strikes Iranian oil tankers as Tehran targets American base in Jordan

title: Tung Chee-hwa: Hong Kong's first leader after British handover to China dies
description: Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's first leader after the city returned to Chinese rule, has died at the age of 89.The former shipping scion took over the rei
body: Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's first leader after the city returned to Chinese rule, has died at the age of 89.The former shipping scion took over the reins from the last British Governor Chris Patten in July 1997 when the UK handed Hong Kong back to China, ending more than 150 years of British control.Tung's rocky tenure was marked by the Asian Financial Crisis, two major epidemics, and historic protests which attracted criticism of his administration. He eventually resigned in 2005.Tung died on Tuesday night surrounded by loved ones, local media reported. His office described him as a man "devoted to his country and its people".Born in Shanghai in 1937, Tung graduated with a mechanical engineering degree from Liverpool University in the UK before moving to the US, where he worked at General Electric for almost a decade.In 1969, he moved to Hong Kong and worked in his father's shipping conglomerate, the Orient Overseas, eventually taking over the reins in 1979.His political career began in 1992 when he was appointed a member of Patten's executive council.Despite having little political experience, Tung was believed to be handpicked by Beijing to lead Hong Kong after the handover. He was seen as a loyalist, especially after China's state-run banks helped rescue his family business during a global slump in the mid-1980s.During a reception at the Great Hall of the People in January 1996, China's then-president Jiang Zemin walked across a packed room to shake Tung's hands – a widely photographed gesture that at the time famously signalled Beijing's backing of Tung for the top job.The Asian Financial Crisis hit shortly after Tung took over, which sent home prices diving. His administration was also beset by a series of public health challenges, including a bird flu outbreak from 1997 to 2002 and the 2003 outbreak of Sars, also known as Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome.But Tung's biggest political challenge took place in July 2003 during his second term, when half a million Hongkongers took to the streets to protest against a proposed national security law they feared would threaten their civic rights.His administration abandoned the proposed legislation following the massive outcry, which also contributed to Tung stepping down in March 2005.At the time his declining health was cited as a reason - but some said he was pressured by Beijing to step down.Beijing ultimately imposed a national security law on Hong Kong in 2020, which authorities have argued is necessary to maintain stability. Critics however have called it "the end of Hong Kong" and say it has created a climate of fear in the city.Tung's last public outing was in July 2021, at an event marking the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Chinese Communist Party. He underwent heart surgery months later, according to reports.He is survived by his wife and three children.Hong Kong's former chief executives have paid tribute to Tung. Leung Chun-ying, who led the city between 2012 and 2017, described him as a "benevolent" leader who "won people over with reason".Carrie Lam, who was the chief executive from 2017 to 2022, said Tung's leadership made "a historic contribution with lasting benefits".China's state news agency Xinhua called Tung a "renowned patriot, distinguished social activist, close friend of the Communist Party of China". It also noted that Tung had served as one of many vice-chairmen of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, China's top political advisory body, for four consecutive terms.

schema.headline: Tung Chee-hwa: Hong Kong's first leader after British handover to China dies

title: US Open 2026 results: Carlos Alcaraz beaten by Ben Shelton in epic quarter-final
description: Carlos Alcaraz's US Open title defence came to an end in a dramatic five-set quarter-final loss to Ben Shelton that ended at 03:34 local time - the la
body: Carlos Alcaraz's US Open title defence came to an end in a dramatic five-set quarter-final loss to Ben Shelton that ended at 03:34 local time - the latest finish in the tournament's history.A large crowd remained captivated deep into the night as a modern classic unfolded over an unpredictable four hours and 28 minutes on Arthur Ashe Stadium.The match did not begin until about 11pm in New York, after the start of the night session was delayed by Tuesday's earlier matches.At its conclusion, eighth seed Shelton basked in a standing ovation from a delirious audience after completing a 6-7 (5-7) 6-1 6-3 1-6 7-6 (10-7) victory that will live long in the memory of all those still present.It was the biggest - and certainly most significant - win of the 23-year-old's career.Shelton had not beaten a top-three player in 17 attempts, and had lost each of his three previous matches against Spain's Alcaraz. It also boosted home hopes of a first American men's singles champion in New York for 23 years.Shelton was not born when Andy Roddick won the US Open in 2003 - but an American finalist is guaranteed when he and Frances Tiafoe meet in Friday's semi-finals.Alcaraz was competing at his first tournament since a lengthy injury lay-off - but that is to take nothing away from Shelton, who produced a phenomenal performance.Seven-time major winner Alcaraz had exceeded expectations on his return after more than four months out with a wrist injury, including sweeping past 20th seed Tommy Paul in straight sets to reach the last eight.But the 23-year-old's lack of match fitness appeared to finally catch up with him in a high-octane encounter filled with breathless exchanges and astounding displays of athleticism.Even when it appeared Alcaraz had emptied the tank, the two-time winner would not only forced a deciding set but go the distance as the players engaged in a tense 10-point match tie-break that provided a fitting conclusion to the contest.

schema.headline: US Open 2026 results: Carlos Alcaraz beaten by Ben Shelton in epic quarter-final

title: Chris Mason: Burnham looks to show he will go further than Starmer with West Bank sanctions
description: There is little doubt that the UK's decision to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank is another significant shift in Britain
body: There is little doubt that the UK's decision to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank is another significant shift in Britain's posture in the Middle East.The announcement from the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, with the Prime Minister Andy Burnham alongside him in the House of Commons, comes almost exactly a year after the UK formally recognised a Palestinian state. And it comes garnished with blunt language about Israel's conduct.This latest announcement is both a logical extension of that decision of 12 months ago, senior figures argue, but also, in words and actions, an expression of Burnham's desire to go further than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer was willing to.It is, Miliband believes, a re-assertion of the logic of eventually arriving at a two-state solution – a viable Palestinian state alongside Israel. The foreign secretary passionately argued that the UK did have agency and could act – and to do nothing would amount to failure. "A strategy of passivity in the face of what is happening is not a strategy," is how Miliband put it in an interview with Jewish News, external. There is a pride among his team that after a diplomatic effort over the summer, there is a breadth to the coordinated international action on this, with 11 other countries, including France and Canada, sharing the same approach."We provided a convening and coordinating role in pulling this together," one source told me, "but we didn't have to convince others to do this. They were coming to the same view themselves, so we agreed we should all go out and say this at the same time."The hope is that coordinated action increases the likelihood that the measures will have an impact and minimises the blowback to any one country from Israel or America.UK officials had anticipated one likely reaction from Israel would be the enforced closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem, which has indeed happened.And while there is a weary acknowledgement that no one can be certain what President Donald Trump might say next about anything ever, it is noted in Whitehall that the initial reaction of the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was pretty understated.As for the domestic political context, plenty in the Labour movement and the wider British left have long clamoured for this to happen. Around 140 Labour MPs went public with this demand at the beginning of the summer, and Burnham was explicit in his criticism of his predecessor's approach to the Middle East, writing in July: "Labour's initial response to the treatment of Gaza caused huge hurt. We got it wrong and I am sorry about that."In recent years Labour has haemorrhaged support in many communities with a significant Muslim population, and so for a new Labour prime minister seeking to lure as many on the left – and beyond – under Labour's umbrella, this diplomatic intervention makes sense.But the reaction of the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, writing in the Jewish Chronicle, external, is a reminder of another challenge for Burnham, both political and societal."Once again, British Jews find themselves warning their own government that its relentless demonisation of the world's only Jewish state risks fanning the flames of antisemitism here at home," Badenoch said.Later, the Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said it was "truly a dark day for Britain's Jews".Last October, as Mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham was the local figurehead during the grim reality of an attack at the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in the city.Miliband has sought to address concerns about what Badenoch calls "demonisation" by making his view clear that "holding British Jews responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, pure and simple".But Labour figures are keenly aware that at points in the last decade, under the leadership of Jeremy Corbyn, the Labour Party's relationship with many British Jews was dire, a situation Starmer sought to rectify as a priority in the early years of his leadership.In other words, the party's recent relations with many British Jews has been fragile for some time - and many in the community already felt vulnerable after last year's attack in Manchester, and the later arson attacks on Jewish community ambulances in north-west London in the spring.Burnham has to manage that anxiety while making the case for the changing stance the government is announcing, in the weeks before he meets many of his international counterparts for the first time.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Burnham looks to show he will go further than Starmer with West Bank sanctions

title: What are my rights if my flight is cancelled or delayed?
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesUpdated 25 minutes agoThousands of air passengers have seen their travel plans disrupted after an air traffic contro
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesUpdated 25 minutes agoThousands of air passengers have seen their travel plans disrupted after an air traffic control problem grounded nearly 2,000 flights across the UK.  When a flight is cancelled or delayed, passengers affected have various rights – such as a refund or be put on another flight. However, these can vary depending on which carrier you are flying with and from where.Only when an airline is at fault - not issues such as air traffic control problems - is extra compensation payable. Here's what it means for you.What do airlines have to offer passengers?When flights are delayed or cancelled, UK and EU airlines, and other carriers when you are departing a UK or EU airport, have a duty to look after you.The reason for the delay or cancellation does not matter. So anyone affected by the air transport delays will be eligible.That includes providing meals and accommodation, if necessary, and getting you to your destination. The airline should organise putting you on an alternative flight, at no extra cost.Additional losses, such as unused accommodation, might require a claim to a credit card provider, if that was the payment option used.After that, a claim may need to go to your travel insurance provider. But there is no standard definition of what is covered.It may require a close look at the details of the policy to see what is covered, and in which circumstances.Passengers are also being urged to heed travel advice from the UK government, external, as this can also affect travel insurance rights.If my flight is cancelled, can I get a refund or another flight?If your flight is covered by UK law, your airline must let you choose between either getting a refund or being booked on to an alternative flight.That's regardless of how far in advance the cancellation was made.You can get your money back for any part of the ticket you have not used.So, if you booked a return flight and the outbound leg is cancelled, you can get the full cost of the return ticket refunded.If you still want to travel, your airline must find you an alternative flight.If another airline is flying to your destination significantly sooner, or there are other suitable modes of transport, then you have a right to be booked on to that alternative transport instead.If your flight was coming into the UK on a non-UK or EU airline, then you should check the terms and conditions of your booking.How do I renew my UK passport and what is the 10-year rule?, externalThree things you can do to stop EU border checks at the airport costing youWill the airline pay for food and accommodation?If you are stuck abroad or at the airport because of a flight cancellation, airlines covered by UK legislation must also provide you with other assistance.This includes:a reasonable amount of food and drink (often in the form of vouchers)a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls)free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next daytransport to and from the accommodationIf your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later.The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary.Civil Aviation Authority: Delays and cancellations, externalYou are entitled to the same assistance as for a cancellation if your flight is delayed by more than two hours for a short-haul flight, three hours for a medium-haul, or four hours for a long-haul.If you are delayed by more than five hours and no longer want to travel, you can get a full refund.What are my rights if I have booked a package holiday?If you booked a package holiday with a company that is an ABTA member and your flight is cancelled, you are entitled to a suitable alternative flight or a full refund.ABTA: What are your rights?, externalCan I claim extra compensation for disruption?Disruption caused by things like air traffic control issues – but also bad weather, strikes by airport staff, or conflict, or other "extraordinary circumstances" – does not entitle you to extra compensation.However, in other circumstances, when it is considered to be the airline's fault, you have a number of rights under UK law, external.These apply as long as you are flying from a UK airport on any airline, arriving at a UK airport on an EU or UK airline, or arriving at an airport in the EU on a UK airline.What you are entitled to depends on what caused the cancellation and how much notice you are given.If your flight is cancelled with less than two weeks' notice, you may be able to claim compensation based on the timings of the alternative flight you are offered.The amount you are entitled to also depends on how far you were travelling:for flights under 1,500km, such as Glasgow to Amsterdam, you can claim up to £220 per personfor flights of 1,500km to 3,500km, such as East Midlands to Marrakesh, you can claim up to £350 per personfor flights over 3,500km, such as London to New York, you can claim up to £520 per personWhat if flight delays mean I am late for work?Airlines will not refund you for loss of earnings. Travel insurance policies will not usually cover loss of earnings either.If you think you're going to be late back at work because of flight delays, you have a responsibility to let your employer know, legal experts say.You should agree with your employer how to deal with the absence – for example, by using annual leave or taking unpaid leave.Employers have no legal obligation to pay employees who are absent in this situation, experts say, unless it is stated in their contract.

schema.headline: What are my rights if my flight is cancelled or delayed?

title: South Park creators rename show 'South America' in apparent dig at Trump
description: The creators of South Park, the animated TV show, have announced that its new series will be named South America, in an apparent reference to US Presi
body: The creators of South Park, the animated TV show, have announced that its new series will be named South America, in an apparent reference to US President Donald Trump's attempts to rename a lake and a gulf."Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA," creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker wrote in a statement. Trump signed an executive order in August to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and last year declared that the Gulf of Mexico be known as the Gulf of America.The announcement from South Park, now in its 29th season, comes after the show won an Emmy for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday.The official name change shared to the show's official social media account featured an image of the South Park sign with the word 'Park' replaced with 'America'."We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount - a Skydance Capitulation," its creators said in the post.Paramount Skydance is the show's parent company. The Trump administration this year approved a $111bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery - one of the biggest media deals in history. But the merger has since been paused until June 2027, after 12 US states filed lawsuits against the deal for fear of it harming competition and leading to higher prices for consumers. A day before the show's announcement, Trump shared an AI-generated video of him placing the word 'America' over 'Mexico' on a "Welcome to New Mexico" sign.In August, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, Trump ordered a similar change for Lake Ontario - renaming it Lake America.Apple and Google subsequently changed the name in their respective Maps apps for US-based users.And last year, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed as Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.South Park, which has run since 1997, has regularly mocked the US president during his two presidency terms.Both its creators, Stone and Parker, have repeatedly drawn criticism from Trump, the White House and MAGA supporters for its jabs at the president. During its 27th season, the White House described South Park as a "fourth-rate" show that was "hanging on by a thread with uninspired ideas in a desperate attempt for attention", after an episode depicted Trump naked in bed with Satan.After winning the award for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday, South Park also shared an image depicting a fictionalised Donald Trump with the words: "You finally got your Emmy."The new season of South Park will premiere on 16 September.

schema.headline: South Park creators rename show 'South America' in apparent dig at Trump

title: Thousands of Neet teens are missing from official stats, report warns
description: There could be tens of thousands more teenagers who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) than official statistics suggest, the children
body: There could be tens of thousands more teenagers who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) than official statistics suggest, the children's commissioner for England has warned.A report by Dame Rachel de Souza said around 42,000 16- and 17-year-olds in England were officially classed as studying at college, but were not showing up at least half of the time.She said they had gone "under the radar" and were "not getting the support that they need".The Department for Education (DfE) said it planned to help colleges track attendance and ultimately to gather that data centrally.Unlike schools, further education and sixth form colleges in England are not required to collect or report attendance data.Dame Rachel's report is based on attendance data obtained from 262 college groups in England and says rates are "substantially lower" than in schools.It suggests that more than half (52.2%) of 16- and 17-year-olds are estimated to be persistently absent by the standards used in schools, meaning they are missing 10% or more of college sessions.And around 42,000 (5.9%) are severely absent, meaning they are missing at least half of college sessions.The DfE estimates that 57,000 16- and 17-year-olds in England are Neet, and Dame Rachel's report argues that these persistently absent teenagers should be considered as "hidden" Neets alongside them.Dame Rachel told the BBC a range of factors led to teenagers missing college, including part-time work and travel costs, and that some had been largely absent from education since the Covid pandemic.She said while those juggling part-time employment were likely to miss college every so often, it was those who are "far more vulnerable" who were likely to be severely absent.She added that it was "shocking" that the DfE did not collect the data as it meant the issue was "ignored"."It's under the radar and these kids are not getting the support that they need," she said.Liam Sloan, principal at Bolton College, said not many students missed more than half of classes, but those who were absent often had mental health challenges or part-time jobs."Sometimes the student being able to be offered that £30 shift there and then means more... than the potential qualification in six or seven months' time," he said.He said there was a particular issue in English and maths GCSE classes, which students in England are required to study alongside other courses if they don't have a grade 4 or above.Attendance rates at the college had improved in recent years though, he said, and this year it has introduced full-time "positive engagement officers" to greet students each morning and contact those who do not show up.Dame Rachel said she expected the government to respond to her recommendations, including:Collecting and setting targets for attendance data for 16- and 17-year-olds"Expediting" the rollout of mental health support teams in collegesImproving work experienceIntroducing free bus travel for childrenApproximately one in eight people aged 16 to 24 are Neet, according to data published by the Office for National Statistics.In May, the first instalment of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn warned that figure could be one in six within five years, and that the country was "at risk of a lost generation."The final instalment is expected to set out recommendations for tackling the problem in the coming weeks.Dame Rachel's report describes "hidden" Neets as those enrolled but persistently absent from college, while Milburn's interim report used it to describe those who are Neet and also not claiming benefits, and are therefore harder to reach.Cath Sezen, director of education policy at the Association of Colleges, said she agreed with many of the report's recommendations but said "funding pressures [were] limiting colleges' ability to provide tailored support"."We have called time and time again for increased investment, better integration of support services and a stronger national strategy for employer engagement," she said.The DfE said students in further education needed to be prioritised in future reforms to help tackle the Neets crisis.A spokesperson also said a new stepping-stone qualification would be brought in to reduce the "endless treadmill" of students failing and resitting GCSE maths and English, and that the government would track attendance in colleges and accelerate the rollout of mental health support teams.

schema.headline: Thousands of Neet teens are missing from official stats, report warns

title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk
description: The work by Oxford University, which is published in the International Journal of Cancer, defines any drink at 65 degrees Celsuis or above as "very ho
body: The work by Oxford University, which is published in the International Journal of Cancer, defines any drink at 65 degrees Celsuis or above as "very hot" and posing a potential risk.Consuming six or more hot drinks per day also raises the risk, according to data from 977,282 middle-aged men and women.Although adding milk can cool drinks down slightly, a milky tea or coffee may still be far too hot, researchers say.Tea made immediately after a kettle is fully boiled is touching boiling point, which is 100 degrees C (212 degrees F). Once poured into a cup, that lowers to around 90 or 95 degrees C.The advice is to wait a few minutes before drinking so the beverage cools to a safer temperature.Cancer Research UK says it's difficult to put an exact time on how long a hot drink should be left to cool."But if you're worried, we'd suggest just waiting until it's comfortable to drink rather than drinking it while it's still very hot," the charity said.Lead researcher Dr Keren Papier said research in South America - where many people drink a very hot herbal beverage called mate - had already shown a similar link between hot drinks and oesophageal cancer.But she said: "More research is now needed to identify the exact drink temperatures linked to this increased risk."A separate study, external of 118 young adults who did multiple tastings of different black coffees found most only deemed the drinks to be too hot if the temperature was 70 degrees C or above. According to one takeaway coffee cup manufacturer, the ideal temperature for hot coffee on the go is between 49 and 60 degrees C. Should a barista want the coffee to stay hotter for longer - if a customer requests extra hot - it can be served at over 82 degrees C, says MTPak Coffee.

schema.headline: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk

title: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony endures for bereaved, 25 years on
description: Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John Resta and his wife SylviaByAlice CuddyThe US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal ac
body: Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John Resta and his wife SylviaByAlice CuddyThe US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history".But a quarter of a century on, the trial of its alleged mastermind is yet to begin and families of those killed fear that time for justice to be delivered is running out.Tom Resta's brother John and his wife Sylvia, who was seven months pregnant, were among the almost 3,000 people killed on 11 September 2001 when hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia. Another crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after the passengers fought back.The couple had been preparing their unborn baby's nursery, painting it with characters from the children's television show Blue's Clues in the days before 9/11. They had dreamed of having a baby and doted on the children of friends and family.On the day of the attacks, the couple - both traders - were working on the 92nd floor of the north tower of the World Trade Center."After all this time, it still chokes me up," Resta told the BBC through tears. While 25 years have passed, he said 9/11 was "almost constantly" on his mind.Resta has been to the US naval base of Guantanamo Bay four times to watch complex pre-trial proceedings for alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and his co-defendants - a process he describes as "laborious and tedious".A military prison was established on the base in south-eastern Cuba during the "war on terror" that followed the 9/11 attacks, and Mohammed - often referred to as KSM - has now been held there for 20 years without ever being convicted.Relatives of victims enter a lottery process to attend the proceedings in a high-security courtroom, where thick glass separates them and members of the press from the defendants.The pre-trial process has been going on for so long that it has now been presided over by five different military judges.Last month, as the 25th anniversary approached, there was a flurry of movement and something of a breakthrough, with a trial date set for Mohammed for June 2028.But Resta said he was bracing himself for further delays, and with so much time having passed, some of his relatives feared they would not live long enough to see the trial."My father will be 98 in November, and I don't think he's expecting to see it. I have a lot of family members - aunts, uncles - that would all like to see it happen. But my parents in particular, I don't think they expect to live long enough," he said."Hopefully all the defendants will still be alive by the time we get to trial. That's a big worry," he added.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A tribute in light above the New York City skyline, at the 2024 anniversary Resta's concerns that a trial could still be further delayed were shared by relatives of other 9/11 victims.Earlier this year, Stephan Gerhardt made his sixth trip to Guantanamo. He said seeing convictions for the death of his younger brother Ralph was vital for him, but something he wished he no longer had to think about."I want to concentrate on the memories," he said.  "I still have Ralph's car. I'm trying to restore it and get it in pristine shape again… We were recently visiting my parents, and we found some of his things that they were holding onto, and the emotion behind it is like, 'yeah, this is just some old stuff, but it belonged to my little brother'."Gerhardt said his "biggest concern" was that he wanted to see Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators convicted before they died."They're getting elderly… I don't want them to pass away without being convicted, because that would be an injustice to all the family members - that we captured these people, but we never got to try them and convict them for the mass murder that they did of our loved ones."Image source, FBIImage caption, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed as he appeared on the FBI's Most Wanted websiteMohammed has been charged with offences including conspiracy and murder, with 2,976 victims listed on the charge sheet. He is accused of conceiving the idea of training pilots to fly commercial planes into buildings and taking those plans to Osama bin Laden, leader of the militant Islamist group al-Qaeda.He has previously said he planned the "9/11 operation from A to Z".But days after the trial date was set for 2028, the military judge threw out confessions made by Mohammed to FBI agents on Guantanamo Bay after he was brought there from secret CIA prisons known as "black sites", which he had been held in for years. In his ruling, the judge described Mohammed's treatment by the CIA as "extraordinary physical and mental abuse".He said the confessions were not voluntary and could not be used against Mohammed at trial.Experts say the torture of Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators has been the main reason for the lengthy delays in the case."Every single issue has been litigated through the issue of torture," said Kasey McCall-Smith, an international law professor at Edinburgh University.She said the defendants were subjected to "years of abuse", including waterboarding and stress positions.Image source, Tom RestaImage caption, John and Sylvia Resta on their wedding dayJohn Ryan, author of America's Trial: Torture and the 9/11 Case on Guantanamo Bay, said last month's ruling means prosecutors lose what they had described as their best evidence against Mohammed, but it is unclear how much it will impact the case.The prosecution has other evidence, Ryan says, including intercepted phone calls and secret recordings, but whether they can feature in the trial is not yet guaranteed. "Mohammad's team and the other defence teams will file motions to suppress some of these categories of evidence, as well."During the George W Bush administration, the US admitted using "enhanced interrogation techniques" to acquire information from suspects but said these methods saved lives and never amounted to torture. President Barack Obama banned them on his second day in office.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, President George W Bush on Air Force One after the attacksRelatives of the victims say the torture of the defendants has so far blocked their right to justice."If we would've not tortured them, the legal implications here would've been much, much simpler. They probably would've been sentenced to death a long time ago," said Gerhardt. "I can't control what the government did, and we've got to live with the impacts."Both Gerhardt and Resta travelled to Guantanamo in early 2025 when Mohammed and two of his co-defendants had been due to plead guilty under a controversial deal struck with US government prosecutors, through which they would not face a death penalty trial.The BBC was with them at the base when the pleas were paused at the last minute after the US government argued that to "deprive the government and the American people of a public trial as to the respondents' guilt and the possibility of capital punishment" would cause "irreparable" harm.Legal wrangling over the validity of the deal is continuing.Some victims' relatives viewed the deal as the only way through, while others criticised it as too lenient and lacking transparency.Resta said he had supported the deal to secure convictions."My philosophy is these guys are not the kind of people that should be out walking the streets, but as far as I'm concerned, they can just stay right where they are.  I just want them convicted," he said.Brett Eagleson, whose dad Bruce was killed in the attacks, said he wanted a full trial, not a plea deal."It's not so much that I'm taking an opinion on life or death for these prisoners, but I believe in the judicial system and I believe that the process works and I believe that a trial and discovery and sort of a public airing is the way to flush the truth out," he said.Image source, Brett EaglesonImage caption, Brett Eagleson was 15 when his father Bruce was killed Eagleson described the situation on Guantanamo as "a mess" and said he had decided not to attend any of the pre-trial proceedings there."My overall feeling is a sense of betrayal from the US government and a sense of extreme frustration," he said. "They've botched every single part of this trial."With 25 years having passed since the attacks, he said that while 9/11 was a constant presence in his own life, to the wider public it was "becoming a historical event"."I think people just assume that we got Bin Laden, we're out of Iraq, the war in Afghanistan's over, and they just assume that chapter has ended."When the trial does eventually start, at a military court at Guantanamo, it has been estimated that it will last about a year.Professor Kasey McCall-Smith said the point of the pre-trial proceedings had been determining "what evidence gets in and what evidence doesn't get in"."If that is agreed in advance, the trial can be more expeditious," she explained.As the relatives of the victims prepared for another anniversary marking the death of their loved ones, Gerhardt said he was looking forward to a time that the trial was over and he no longer had to think about or travel to Guantanamo."It's a place I don't want to come back to. I want to live my life, enjoy my passions and my memories of Ralph," he said.

schema.headline: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony endures for bereaved, 25 years on

title: US slaps import ban on Canadian alcohol, motorbikes and other goods
description: The US is banning a slew of Canadian products, including alcoholic spirits, dairy goods and motorbikes, as its neighbour's retaliatory tariffs on Amer
body: The US is banning a slew of Canadian products, including alcoholic spirits, dairy goods and motorbikes, as its neighbour's retaliatory tariffs on American goods come into force.In a series of executive orders on Tuesday, President Donald Trump said Canada is "discriminating" against the US and outlined the import bans, which will begin on 29 September.Earlier on Tuesday, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video address that his country's move away from the US as its largest trading partner "will come at a cost".Both US and Canadian officials have said they would like to strike a trade deal, but no new talks have been scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August.The BBC has contacted Carney's office for comment.The White House's new sanctions are the latest strike in a months-long trade war between the US and Canada. The two countries have historically been close allies, with each a key business partner to the other.Generally more than two-thirds of Canada's total exports go to its neighbour.On the other hand, Canada is the second-largest trading partner of the US, after Mexico, although its exports are far more diversified.Business owners on both sides of the border have expressed fears over the trade war's fallout. Many expect prices of goods to rise and the number of customers to fall.Last month, the White House imposed 50% tariffs on around $20bn (£14.8bn) of Canadian goods after several rounds of talks had broken down.Those tariffs hit sectors including Canada's furniture and wine industries, as well as some sporting and fishing equipment businesses.Canada responded with dollar-for-dollar tariffs on US goods like steel, clothing and furniture. The counter-duties came into effect after midnight on Tuesday.Canada is "discriminating" against US businesses by restricting American goods while not doing the same to the same products from other countries, the White House said when announcing the new import restrictions on Tuesday.Some products, like whey and non-alcoholic beer, have been banned from import entirely, while tariffs have been further hiked for others, including cheeses and motorboats.Washington has targeted "significant industries" for Canada, including its politically influential dairy businesses, said economics lecturer Scott French from the University of New South Wales in Australia.Trump has previously argued that Canada's system - which has production quotas, set pricing, and import limits on dairy, eggs, and poultry - is unreasonable to US farmers.The import bans and new tariffs will also put Canada's leaders under more pressure to resist Trump's demands for concessions, French said.The trade war will be "costly for both sides due to the historical level of integration of the North American economy," he said, adding that consumers on both sides will end up as "the biggest losers".On Monday, Trump hinted at more trade restrictions to come, warning Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it would no longer be able to sell its products in the US unless it moves manufacturing there.Trump has long believed that tariffs will help reduce trade imbalances between the US and other countries, but his wide-ranging levies have upset many of the States' traditional allies.Some Canadians have led a massive boycott of US products like alcohol, which have vanished from some store shelves after Trump launched his global tariff campaign last year.Trade expert Deborah Elms, from the Hinrich Foundation, told the BBC the import ban could have a "strong" impact on any Canadian business with US buyers, though early estimates show a "modest impact" affecting around $1bn worth of goods.Canada will likely "hold course for now" and adjust their business support measures to account for the US' latest moves, Elms said."The bigger question is what it will take for the two sides to sit back down together. The language in these proclamations, as an example, isn't helpful in getting to the negotiating table," she added.

schema.headline: US slaps import ban on Canadian alcohol, motorbikes and other goods

title: Trent Alexander-Arnold: Real Madrid right-back returns to midfield
description: In the middle again - but Mourinho says Alexander-Arnold 'not a midfielder'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Trent Alexander-Arnold started for
body: In the middle again - but Mourinho says Alexander-Arnold 'not a midfielder'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Trent Alexander-Arnold started for only the second time this season in the win over Inter MilanByElizabeth ConwaySpanish football reporter at the BernabeuIt's the question that just doesn't seem to go away - can Trent Alexander-Arnold really work in midfield?Gareth Southgate played him there for England during Euro 2024 before ending the experiment after only two group games.Much of Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool gameplan relied on his ability to step into the middle and spray passes around... albeit from a starting position of right-back.And now Jose Mourinho has become the latest manager to dabble, picking the 27-year-old in midfield for Real Madrid's Champions League win over Inter Milan on Tuesday.Having struggled to establish himself as Real's first-choice full-back since moving to the Bernabeu last summer, could this be the moment he finally clicks in the middle of the park?"He has played midfield with England and Liverpool... but he is not a midfielder," insisted Mourinho after his side's edgy 2-1 win."He has played very well. He has interpreted what he needed to really well, tactically."Both him and Valverde have worked very well at this level."So while Mourinho was "very grateful" for Alexander-Arnold's efforts in the middle, don't expect to see him play there on a regular basis.The former Liverpool player's inclusion in midfield was largely circumstantial, with suspensions for Eduardo Camavinga, Arda Guler and Bernardo Silva leaving Mourinho short on options.Alexander-Arnold lined up alongside Federico Valverde but had a mixed evening, creating two chances and attempting more crosses than any other Real player - but failing to win a tackle. His passing accuracy was also down at 83.3%.He was substituted shortly after Inter pulled one back on 77 minutes, prompting whistles around the stadium - although this could well have been frustration Madrid supporters felt at their team's performance rather than at Alexander-Arnold individually.It was the first competitive match in which Alexander-Arnold and fellow right-back Denzel Dumfries had started together. He started both for a pre-season friendly against Fiorentina, with Alexander-Arnold operating at right-back while Dumfries played further forward on the same side.It is clear Mourinho still doesn't have a definite starting right-back, so in the same way Alexander-Arnold had to fight to start with Dani Carvajal last season, he is doing the same this season with Dumfries.But BBC Sport understands the Portuguese has been impressed by the England international's performances, values and the versatility he brings to the squad.Indeed, Mourinho views Alexander-Arnold as different from many traditional full-backs because of his ability to move into central areas and contribute to attacks from midfield positions.His passing, crossing, through balls and set-piece delivery remain among the strongest parts of his game.'He left the pitch with nothing left to give'While Southgate's attempts to convert him into a central player at Euro 2024 ultimately ended in him being dropped from the team, Alexander-Arnold has had some success there in the past.In June 2023, he was handed the England number 10 shirt for a qualifier in Malta, a game which the Three Lions won 4-0 - and in which Alexander-Arnold himself scored from midfield."I haven't played it too much, but it feels comfortable," the 24-year-old told Channel 4 when asked whether this was a position he could see his future in."It feels natural, I will say that. It's somewhere I can see myself playing."Southgate continued to flirt with playing him in that position during the course of the next 12 months, before abandoning the plan after an underwhelming 1-1 draw with Denmark. Alexander-Arnold was brought off before the hour-mark.After Tuesday's win over Inter, Mourinho admitted the position still caused some difficulties."He has lost some balls because it is not the same to play in this position compared to at right-back," he said."The intensity of physical work is quite difficult. He has a different engine. He has given 100%. He left the pitch with nothing left to give."Watch highlights of every Champions League game from 22:00 on Wednesday on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app.There will also be a Champions League Match of the Day on BBC One on Wednesday, from 22:40 to 00:00.

schema.headline: Trent Alexander-Arnold: Real Madrid right-back returns to midfield

title: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Olivia Rodrigo was the last act to perform on the Pyramid Stage in 2025, before Glastonbury took a fallow yearByMusic
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Olivia Rodrigo was the last act to perform on the Pyramid Stage in 2025, before Glastonbury took a fallow yearByMusic correspondentAfter taking a fallow year in 2026, the Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's event will go on sale in October.Tickets for the weekend will cost £408 including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from 2025.Headliners for the festival, which takes place from 23 to 27 June, have yet to be announced, but rumours are already swirling, with everyone from Harry Styles and Fontaines DC to Taylor Swift and Stevie Wonder said to be in the mix.Tickets for the festival typically sell out in less than an hour, with thousands of fans  joining online queues to fight for their place.In a post on the official Glastonbury Instagram page, external, organisers said tickets with coach travel would go on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday, 1 October.General admission tickets go on sale a couple of days later, at 09:00 BST on Sunday 4 October.As part of an ongoing campaign to stop touts, anyone wanting to attend Glastonbury had to be registered in advance. You can check your registration on its website. , externalIn recent years, the festival has also introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.Festival prices rise across the boardGlastonbury, which features more than 100 stages, was already the UK's most expensive music festival, but next year's ticket prices are the highest ever - breaking the £400 barrier for the first time.The increase is part of a pattern across the industry.Analysis by BBC News found the cost of attending the UK's major festivals has surged over the past decade - rising above the rate of inflation.Parklife tickets have increased by around £69 (71%) in real terms since 2013 - while Reading and Leeds had a much smaller increase, rising by about £40 (14%) over the same period.In the same period, Glastonbury's ticket prices went up by about £85  - a 30% price hike.The price hikes have multiple causes - from increased energy and infrastructure costs to post-Brexit labour shortages. However, last weekend's Reading and Leeds festival held prices at their 2025 level, with passes costing £325, rising to £361 with early-bird entry.Glastonbury said they would not be commenting on today's announcement but, in 2023, Emily Eavis acknowledged it was a "challenging time" for festival organisers."We have tried very hard to minimise the increase in price on the ticket but we're facing enormous rises in the costs of running this vast show, whilst still recovering from the huge financial impact of two years without a festival because of Covid."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Madonna has hinted that she will perform in the UK next year, but has not said whereThe festival last took place in 2025, with Olivia Rodrigo, The 1975 and Neil Young topping the bill.Glastonbury organiser Emily Eavis recently scotched rumours that Madonna would be among the headliners for next year's event."No, it's definitely not Madonna, I'll tell you that," she told BBC Radio 4's PM programme."But we have got three [other] headliners and we're very excited about it - it's all coming together really well," she added.Asked about the possibility of a performance from Taylor Swift, Eavis laughed and said she didn't want to discuss the line-up any more.

schema.headline: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price

title: I'm 27 and I've already written my will - here's why
description: Writing a will is probably not on the to-do lists of most 27-year-olds. But Erin Atkinson has already decided what should happen to her money and belo
body: Writing a will is probably not on the to-do lists of most 27-year-olds. But Erin Atkinson has already decided what should happen to her money and belongings when she dies."At first it felt quite surreal because you associate wills with older people," she says.Erin works in psychological research at a London university and moved to the capital from Bristol four years ago. She now rents and, although she did not want to share her exact salary, does not see herself as particularly wealthy. Even so, she has already decided where some of her things should go.Her £7,000 car will go to her sister. A gold necklace given to her by her partner will go back to him. And she has asked for some of her money to go to a cause that matters deeply to her."One thing that's close to my heart is an endometriosis charity," she says."It felt really empowering that I could have that written down to say I want X amount donated."The 2025 National Wills Report found that just one in five 18 to 24-year-olds has a will in place. That rises to 33% of 22 to 34-year-olds, compared with 56% of people aged over 55.Writing a will can seem daunting and expensive. But there are ways to get one written for free or at a lower cost. For example, every November, Will Aid, external works with solicitors who volunteer their time and waive their fee for writing a basic will.Members of a trade union may also benefit from a free will writing service, according to Citizens Advice., externalFor many young people, making a will may not seem necessary, particularly if they feel they have little to leave behind.Sophia Maslin, founder of Morby, a website that allows people to create wills online, says the idea that you need to own a lot before making a will is one of the biggest misconceptions she comes across."People believe they don't own enough. But actually, if you've got some sort of savings, investments, pensions, your social media accounts, if you've got pets, even funeral wishes, these are all things to think about," she says.For Erin, the idea of making a will first came up when her friend bought a home.Then she began seeing Maslin talking about wills on TikTok. Maslin had shared the story of her cousin, who died young without a will, and how complicated things became for her family.

schema.headline: I'm 27 and I've already written my will - here's why

title: Lindsay Clancy jurors speak out on what led to mistrial
description: The identities of the nine women and three men on the jury have not been made public and the judge banned any photographing or filming of them during
body: The identities of the nine women and three men on the jury have not been made public and the judge banned any photographing or filming of them during the trial to retain their anonymity. But in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose whether or not to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations. Jurors often choose to speak out - some even write books - after high-profile cases like that of Clancy. The BBC, which was in the court during the case, has confirmed the three women who spoke with NBC were on the jury panel. In the interview with the local Boston NBC affiliate NBC10, which aired on Tuesday, the jury foreperson - a retired fifth-grade teacher - called not being able to reach a verdict in the case "awful" and an "emotional roller coaster". A foreperson acts as a spokesperson for a jury in any US legal case, meaning they are the person delivering a verdict and sending notes to the judge on behalf of the 12-person panel. She said the deliberations were difficult and filled with "lots of crying" and "lots of tears and then hugging". "I was so sad, so sad that we couldn't come up with a verdict for Lindsay. It was so heartbreaking," she added. Throughout the interview, the three women said the jury was in nearly unanimous agreement to enter their verdict but the holdout juror would not change his mind. The foreperson said the lone juror "admitted he had reasonable doubt and I started filling out the forms, I was so excited". She was halfway through filling out the verdict sheets when the holdout juror, who she said was a man, continued: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity," she says he told the panel. The man in question has not come forward and has not responded to these comments. The three jurors noted their deliberations led to fights and yelling, which at times could be heard through the walls. Under Massachusetts law, there was no burden on Clancy to prove her mental illness and that she lacked criminal responsibility. Rather, it was on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt she was criminally responsible when she killed her children, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon previously told the BBC."We weren't trying to figure out if she murdered the children. She did and she's admitted that," the foreperson explained in the interview with NBC. "We're trying to figure out - did she know right from wrong at that time."The three jurors noted they didn't feel persuaded by the prosecution. "Everything proved that she loved her children so she had to have snapped and not known what she was doing," the foreperson said.Another juror, who does work for a government defence contractor, said the holdout juror had questions about what medication Clancy was on."We had the toxicology reports. We could see exactly the amounts," she said, adding that there were nurses on the jury who spoke about that. "He just completely disregarded the information that they gave," the juror added.The third juror, a chef at a senior centre, said she found the prosecutors in the case to be "very, very harsh", adding: "They had no character witness in regard to Lindsay of being a bad mother."Throughout the trial, prosecutors called dozens of witnesses, including several doctors, seeking to prove Clancy had made a calculated decision to murder her children in the basement of their Massachusetts home. The grim case led to a series of dramatic twists and turns as the jury deliberated for nearly 40 hours over seven days to determine Clancy's fate. They signalled multiple times they were facing a deadlock - and at one point told the judge that one member of the panel was not following the judge's instructions on reasonable doubt.The development led to Clancy's defence attorney requesting the holdout juror be removed from the panel - a request that was quickly denied - before the panel again said they could not come to a unanimous decision. Judge William Sullivan then declared a mistrial on Friday. The mistrial leaves both the case and Clancy's future uncertain, as prosecutors determine whether they want to take the case to trial a second time with a new jury. Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has since said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors so the case doesn't see a second trial. The three jurors told NBC they hoped there wasn't a second trial - but if there is - all three said they plan to attend in support of Clancy.

schema.headline: Lindsay Clancy jurors speak out on what led to mistrial

title: Alan Carr holds back tears on special night at National Television Awards
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The comedian was surprised with a top NTA honourByLola SchroerCulture reporterYou can see a full list of winn
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The comedian was surprised with a top NTA honourByLola SchroerCulture reporterYou can see a full list of winners at the bottom of this articleAlan Carr had an emotional night at the 31st National Television Awards on Tuesday as he received the Special Recognition prize following a whirlwind year for the comedian. The London audience had just been treated to a Traitors-themed musical performance in his honour, which included fellow cast member Paloma Faith emerging from a coffin, when he was given the surprise award.Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet before the ceremony, Carr had played down his chances of winning for his semi-autobiographical comedy Changing Ends.He joked: "Comedy is so subjective... Mrs Brown's Boys wins every year, why am I even here?"Figure caption, Watch: 'I still felt bad about Paloma', says Alan CarrCarr was right - Mrs Brown's Boys went on to win the Comedy prize. But the night was just beginning. The Celebrity Traitors favourite had predicted there would be "ugly crying" if he did take home a prize - and he stayed true to his word as he accepted the Special Recognition award, the only category not voted for by the public.Carr told BBC News that being part of The Celebrity Traitors had brought him a level of attention he had never experienced before."I've never had popularity like it," he said, describing the show as a "phenomenon".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Celebrity Traitors won an award after a critically-acclaimed series Carr had more reason to celebrate when The Celebrity Traitors beat the original version of the show to win the Reality Competition prize.His co-star, singer Charlotte Church, praised the show's final, which attracted 15 million viewers within seven days, describing it as a "beautiful vignette of male tenderness and emotional expression"."Alan, Nick (Mohammed) and David (Olusoga), you were just absolutely sublime," she added.Sir David Attenborough wins an NTA at 100Another big win went to Sir David Attenborough, who was named Best Presenter in his 100th birthday year, beating popular duo Ant and Dec, whose 23-year winning streak was broken by Gary Lineker last year.While not in attendance, Attenborough's long-time collaborator Mark Brownlow accepted the award on his behalf and shared a message from the broadcaster urging people to help protect the planet."Humanity has always needed the natural world for all the practicalities of life and for our mental wellbeing," Attenborough wrote. "Now the natural world needs us too: surely we must not ignore that simple fact."Clarkson's Farm wins againClarkson's Farm won an NTA for the second year running, taking the inaugural Celebrity-Led Reality Docuseries award.The new category also featured shows from Stacey Solomon and Joe Swash, Tyson Fury, Kelvin Fletcher, and Bob Mortimer and Paul Whitehouse.Celebrity-led programmes still featured in the Authored Documentary category, with documentaries from Olympian Sir Chris Hoy, former Little Mix singer Jesy Nelson, and Sharon Osbourne's film about her late husband Ozzy among the nominees.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, It was a win for a second year in a row for Jeremy Clarkson Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet, their daughter Kelly Osbourne said her family were "honoured" that the documentary about her father had been nominated, describing it as a "tragic but beautiful story".She said she had spoken to her mother Sharon just before arriving at the ceremony: "We are so close. I was on the phone with her before I got out of the car."In the end, the public chose Our Girls: The Southport Families. The BBC programme followed the families of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, who were murdered at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport in 2024.Accepting the award, Elsie's mother Jenni Stancombe told the audience: "We never expected to be stood up here, so I don't know what to say."We know you didn't vote for us, you voted for our three girls."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The parents of the Southport attack victims were recognised for their powerful film documenting the lives of their daughters 'We are dominating that category'In the drama categories, Vicky McClure won Best Drama Performance for her role in crime thriller Trigger Point, from the first all-female shortlist in the category's history.She told BBC News in the winners' room: "Over the years it has not been our space, and here we are dominating that category."I feel honoured to be amongst those wonderful women."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Vicky McClure came out on top in a list of nominees dominated by female actors Among those nominated alongside McClure was Sheridan Smith for her portrayal of campaigner Ann Ming in ITV true crime drama I Fought The Law.While Smith missed out on the individual prize, I Fought The Law went on to win New Drama.Norton dusts off his Swift-Kelce wedding suitAway from the awards, nominee Graham Norton revealed his red carpet outfit had already had one high-profile outing this year."This is what I wore to Taylor Swift's wedding," he told BBC News.Norton said guests had agreed not to reveal details of the celebrations. "I had a wonderful time and we all agreed by saying yes to going, we weren't going to blab about it."Norton, who also featured in Swift's music video for Opalite earlier this year, said working with the singer showed him "what leadership is like at that level"."It was such a happy set. Everyone was working as hard as they could for her," he said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Graham Norton revealed he wore the same suit to the NTAs as he did to Taylor Swift's weddingThe National Television Awards in full -
